title: Equality
tagline: The meaning of equality and its legal, social, political and economic kinds.

overview.intro: Equality is the claim that human beings ought to be treated as in some respect the same, and every political doctrine is recognisable by what it says that respect is. This unit examines the meaning of equality and the fallacy of treating it as identity, then the four kinds — legal, political, social and economic — and the central problem of whether equality of treatment is compatible with inequality of outcome.

learningOutcomes: Define equality and distinguish it from uniformity.
Describe legal, political, social and economic equality.

Assess the arguments for and against economic equality.
Relate equality to liberty in political argument.

blocks.text: Equality in politics does not mean that people are alike — no serious thinker has claimed that — but that they are to be treated as equal in some specified respect. Aristotle’s formula states the point precisely: justice requires that equals be treated equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their relevant difference. The formula matters because it turns equality into a test rather than a slogan: before demanding equal treatment one must identify the respect in which the cases are equal and confirm that no relevant difference separates them.

Equality must therefore be distinguished from uniformity. Identical treatment of people in different positions may be the grossest inequality — paying a nurse and a manager the same wage is not equality but indifference to difference. Conversely, treating people differently in order to make them equal in capacity, as remedial education does, is equality properly understood. The concept also carries a moral dimension: equal concern and respect means that each person counts for as much as any other in the calculation of public policy, which is why inequalities that treat some lives as incidental are resented whatever their economic effect.

items: Equality is a standard of treatment, not a claim of identity.
Aristotle’s formula makes relevant difference the test of equal treatment.
Uniformity is the caricature; equality often requires unequal treatment to be real.
Equal concern and respect is the moral core behind all four kinds.

blocks.text: Legal equality is equality before the law: the same rules applied to everyone in the same circumstances, no privileged classes or hereditary immunities, and the same access to the courts and procedures that enforce rights. Its landmarks are the abolition of feudal privilege, the extension of the franchise and the guarantee of equal protection. Its practical content is substantial — a person without legal equality can be taxed, detained or dispossessed without remedy — but it is formal by nature, since identical rules applied to people in radically different positions produce results that are equal in form and unequal in effect.

Political equality is equality in the machinery of collective decision: one person, one vote, equal value of each vote, the right to stand for office, and equal access to political organisation and public criticism. Its classic expression is the secret ballot and the universal franchise, and its enemies are property qualifications, communal electorates weighted unequally, and the manipulation of boundaries. Political equality matters instrumentally as well as intrinsically, since a government that must face equal voters is restrained in a way that one answerable to a narrow electorate is not; but the growth of expensive campaigning and media control shows that formal political equality can coexist with large practical inequality of influence.

blocks.text: Social equality concerns standing in the community: the absence of graded hierarchy in status, dignity, dress and manners, and the equal treatment of persons regardless of caste, sex, birth or creed. It is the kind most resistant to legislation, since it lives in habit rather than in law, though law can remove the structures that sustain it — untouchability, segregated facilities, unequal access to education — and social movements can change the habits law cannot reach. Its importance is that unequal status corrodes political and legal equality from below: a group treated as inferior in the bazaar will be treated as inferior at the ballot box and in the court.

Economic equality concerns the distribution of income, wealth and opportunity. Absolute equality of holdings has few serious advocates, since it would abolish the incentives that production requires and would need a coercive apparatus to enforce. The live questions are how wide a distribution a society will tolerate and what floor it guarantees: equality of opportunity demands that talent be able to rise regardless of birth, which requires common schooling, anti-discrimination law and inheritance restraint, while equality of result demands redistribution that directly narrows differences. The debate with liberty runs through it — compulsion is needed to compress outcomes, and the compulsion restricts the liberty of some — but the counter-argument is that destitution is itself a restriction of freedom, so the two cannot be ranked without specifying amounts.

blocks.caption: Four kinds of equality compared

blocks.text: Equality of opportunity is the form of equality on which most political traditions can agree: positions and rewards should be open to all according to ability and effort rather than birth, connection or creed. Its radical form demands that starting points be levelled, since children of wealth inherit tutors, networks and second chances that effort alone cannot offset; its formal version demands only that no artificial barrier be placed in anyone’s way. The distinction matters, because formal opportunity leaves the initial inequality untouched while substantive opportunity requires intervention in family, school and inheritance — which shows that opportunity and outcome cannot be fully separated.

The assessment should credit both sides. Equality of standing is indispensable to liberty: legal privilege and hereditary office destroy freedom for those beneath them, and every durable expansion of liberty has been accompanied by an expansion of equality. Yet equality pursued without limit produces uniformity, coercive machinery and reduced incentives, as the twentieth century demonstrated in economies that abolished private initiative. The defensible position is one of bounded inequality: sufficient equality of status, law and basic capability that freedom is real for everyone, combined with tolerable differences in reward, and a continuous public argument about where the balance lies. The answer that earns the highest marks is one that states which kind of equality is at issue in each case, since the kinds pull in different directions and conflating them is the commonest error.

keyPoints: Equality means equal treatment in a specified respect, not identity between persons.
Aristotle’s formula: treat equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to difference.
Uniformity is the caricature of equality; real equality may require different treatment.
Legal equality is equal rules and access to remedy, but is formal in nature.
Political equality is one person, one vote, with equal value and freedom to organise.
Social equality concerns status and dignity and is the hardest to change by legislation.
Economic equality concerns distribution, with few advocates of absolute equality.

questions.prompt: State the four kinds of equality and give the content of each.
questions.answer: The four kinds are legal, political, social and economic. Legal equality is equality before the law — the same rules for everyone and equal access to the courts. Political equality is equal influence in collective decisions: one person, one vote of equal value, the right to stand for office and freedom to organise. Social equality is the absence of graded hierarchy in status and dignity, regardless of caste, sex, birth or creed. Economic equality concerns the distribution of income, wealth and opportunity, and in practice concerns how wide a difference a society will tolerate and what floor it guarantees.
questions.explanation: All four kinds must be named with content, not merely listed.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between equality of opportunity and equality of result.
questions.answer: Equality of opportunity holds that positions and rewards should be open to all according to ability and effort rather than birth, connection or creed. In its formal version it requires only that no artificial barrier be placed in anyone’s way, leaving inherited differences of circumstance untouched. In its substantive version it requires starting points to be levelled, since wealth, tutoring and networks shape outcomes as much as talent, and this demands common schooling, anti-discrimination law and restraint of inherited advantage. Equality of result is a different claim altogether: it seeks to narrow the distribution of outcomes themselves through redistribution, regardless of differences in effort or talent. The two diverge because substantive opportunity already requires intervention in distribution, while result-equality pushes far beyond it, and result-equality also raises the objection that enforcement requires a coercive apparatus that restricts liberty. The distinction matters because arguments about equality are usually arguments about one of the three positions and are commonly confused.
questions.explanation: Three positions must be distinguished — formal opportunity, substantive opportunity and result — with the practical measures each implies.

questions.prompt: Examine the relationship between equality and liberty.
questions.answer: The relationship depends first on which kinds are in question, and the four kinds of equality pull in different directions relative to liberty. Legal and political equality are its allies without qualification: equality before the law abolishes privileged classes whose immunity is precisely the denial of others’ freedom, and equal voting gives each person a share in the authority that binds them, so that the great expansions of liberty in modern history — abolition of property qualifications, universal suffrage, anti-discrimination law — were at the same time expansions of equality. Social equality works similarly, since a hierarchy of status denies dignity and restricts the associations in which free persons move. Economic equality is where the conflict is said to arise: liberty to accumulate leaves differences that widen without limit, while compressing differences requires taxation and regulation that restrict the liberty of those whose holdings are trimmed, and Hayek’s version adds that planning to equalise necessarily concentrates power and reduces the liberty of all. The counter-argument is that extreme inequality produces unfreedom of its own — destitution excludes a person from contract, travel and the market that formal liberty presupposes, and unlimited wealth can purchase political influence that nullifies the equal vote. The resolution is to specify degrees: up to a point equality of status, education and security makes liberty real for everyone and restricts the liberty of none in any politically significant way, while beyond that point compulsion and uniformity begin to destroy both. The best answers therefore refuse the abstract question, name the kind of equality in issue each time, and judge by whether a given arrangement leaves each person with real capacity to act.
questions.explanation: Full marks require all four kinds of equality distinguished, both the alliance and the conflict argued with evidence, and a judgement stated in terms of degrees rather than absolutes.

questions.prompt: Is equality of opportunity a coherent political demand? Discuss.
questions.answer: The case that it is incoherent begins with the observation that opportunity and outcome are not separable. Every position has a finite number of places, so giving one person a genuinely open opportunity is by definition an opportunity denied to another; to equalise opportunity is therefore already to allocate outcomes, and the demand to level starting points requires decisions about income, schooling, parenting and inheritance that reach far into distribution. A stronger version of the objection holds that talent and effort are themselves unequally distributed by luck — birth, temperament, health — so a race that is perfectly open will still produce radically unequal finishers, at which point the advocate must either accept the inequality, which seems to abandon equality, or correct it, which turns opportunity into result. The case for coherence answers at three levels. First, the demand is comparative and institutional rather than metaphysical: it asks that positions be allocated by demonstrated ability and effort instead of birth, connection or creed, which is a perfectly determinate rule even though it cannot abolish luck. Second, the distinction has practical content, since societies differ enormously on the measures it implies — hereditary office and segregated schooling on one side, common schooling and anti-discrimination enforcement on the other — and those differences are what the demand is used to argue about. Third, the requirement can be specified by domain: equal access to education, to credit and to public office can be secured without fixing the distribution of all rewards, which keeps the demand within reach of ordinary policy. The most defensible judgement is that the demand is coherent as a standard for institutions and incoherent as a promise about results: properly stated, it requires that the rules of allocation be free from arbitrary privilege and that the capacities needed to compete be publicly supplied, while accepting that unequal outcomes will follow from equal rules applied to unequal persons. Marks are awarded for seeing that the apparent paradox comes from treating opportunity as a total condition rather than as a constraint on rules, and for stating precisely which measures the demand does and does not entail.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the incoherence argument in its strongest form, three distinct replies, and a judgement specifying exactly what equality of opportunity requires of institutions.
